title: Statement on AI
text:
In the age where AI is increasingly involved not only in an academic setting, but also in our daily lives, it is both important and necessary to create and follow a personal policy regarding one’s AI use.
There are generally four outcomes when we are faced with a problem in which we might consider using AI to solve (Cipolli 2026). We can decide against using AI at all, verify its suggestions with our own background knowledge, blindly follow it towards a correct answer, or blindly follow it towards an incorrect answer. I believe that relying on AI for answers where we don’t completely understand its sources, methods, or concepts will lead to a society in which humans will lose their autonomy in the workforce, and eventually in their own lives. If we don’t do our own thinking, then our functions in the workplace and in academics will become obsolete.
However, using AI to help us overcome barriers, unexpected issues, or to explain certain concepts that help us along the way of solving a problem can be super beneficial. Rather than spending hours trying to fix a bug that human error may miss, AI can quickly scan an entire file and notice one wrong button that was pressed. Using AI to make our lives more efficient to pave the way for learning, rather than doing the learning for us, is a great way to become an ethical statistical practitioner, as mentioned in the Ethical Guidelines for Statistical Practice (American Statistical Association 2022).
Not only does unethical AI use harm us, it also indirectly harms the people who might rely on our work. Passing work done by AI as your own is both an issue of plaigiarism and responsibility, and others might trust and cite your work as authentic and true, when in reality they are now citing AI (American Statistical Association 2022). It is important that we stay honest with the people we collaborate with and disclose all AI use, with plans to remedy any instances of unethical AI use.




References

American Statistical Association. 2022. Ethical Guidelines for Statistical Practice. Committee on Professional Ethics.


Cipolli, William. 2026. AI Statement.

title: HW1
text:
A benefit of using the Wilcox signed rank test is that the researchers don’t have to assume normality for the underlying population distribution, as that is unknown and the sample size is not large enough for the CLT. However, there are a few concerns to using this test:

The data collected are proportions that represent the number of times the GWL dogs correctly retrieved the new toy when requested out of 12 requests. The fact that this data is discrete with only 13 possible unique observations leads to multiple tied observations in the data. Using the exact Wilcoxon distribution could be an issue due to having many ties, and the authors would need to account for them in order to use an accurate Wilcoxon distribution.
Due to n=10, the sample size is likely not large enough to use an asymptotic distribution because n would usually need to be at least 50. Because the authors didn’t specify which distribution they used, this could be an issue.
The boundedness of the range of the data (0, 1), and the fact that 4 dogs had a proportion of 1.000 is a concern for the symmetry assumption for the Wilcoxon signed rank test. We don’t know the underlying distribution, and we definitely don’t have evidence supporting that it might be symmetric from the sample data.

A one-sample t-test is constrained by the assumption that the population is normally distributed and the population variance exists, both of which we don’t know, and the sample size of n = 10 does not satisfy the CLT. Since the sample data is skewed left, we don’t have evidence that the population distribution is normally distributed from the sample data. Moreover, a one-sample z-test for proportions also does not have a sample size large enough for the CLT. Due to the issues with the sample size, I think the best choice would be to use an exact binomial test because we don’t have to worry about our population data being normally distributed or about the CLT (relies on the binomial distribution). We can frame the data to be Bernoulli by interpreting each dog as a success if it retrieved the new toy correctly more than 50% of the time.



We are aiming to evaluate whether GWL dogs can correctly retrieve a new toy when requested better than chance (50%), aftering overhearing two people reference the object while not addressing the dog. n = 10 dogs were requested 12 times to retrieve the new toy, and our data present the proportion of times the dog correctly retrieved it.
Our null hypothesis is that H0: p = 0.50 and Ha: p > 0.50 and conducting a one-sided exact binomial test using alpha = 0.05, where a success means that the dog retrieved the new toy correctly more than half the time. We decided to use the exact binomial test because we violate no assumptions; our data does not satisfy the normality/CLT condition for a one-sample t-test, does not satisfy the symmetric assumption for a Wilcox signed rank test, and does not satisfy the sample size / CLT condition for a one-sample z-test for proportions.


Code
dat.dogs <- c(1.0000, 1.0000, 0.7500, 1.0000, 0.4167, 0.8333, 0.7500, 0.8333, 0.8333, 1.0000) # data 

successes <- sum(dat.dogs > 0.50)    # counts dogs better than chance (p > 0.50)
n <- length(dat.dogs)                # sample size (number of dogs)

test.result <- binom.test(x = successes,            # number of successes (p > 0.50)
                          n = n,                    # sample size (trials)
                          p = 0.50,                 # p0 = 0.50
                          alternative = "greater")  # one-sided test
(test.stat <- test.result$statistic) # test statistic


number of successes 
                  9 


Code
(p_val <- test.result$p.value)       # p-value


[1] 0.01074219


Code
(CI    <- test.result$conf.int)      # 95% confidence interval


[1] 0.6058367 1.0000000
attr(,"conf.level")
[1] 0.95


Our p-value (p_val = 0.0107) is less than alpha = 0.05, and we have statistically discernible evidence to conclude that the true proportion of correct retrievals is greater than 0.50. We can say with 95% confidence that the true proportion of correct retrievals of the new toy out of 12 requests lies between [0.61, 1.00].

title: HW1
text:
2 Question 2

2.1 Part a
The major issue with the binomial test here is that the number of trials is very low, in addition to already having a low sample size of n = 10. This might decrease the accuracy of the binomial distribution at predicting the true proportion of correctly selecting the new toy when requested. The conditions of the exact binomial test require that there be a fixed number of trials (2), and that each trial ends in a success or a failure. Additionally, the trials must be independent from one another, which is not satisfied in the 2 new toy trials, but would be satisfied if measuring the overall success of each dog as a separate 10 trials. Lastly, the binomial test assumes that the probability of success is the same across each trial, which is assumed to be p = 0.50.


2.2 Part b


Code
dat.dogs2 <- rep(1, 10) # data

n2 <- length(dat.dogs2)  # sample size
successes2 <- sum(dat.dogs2 == 1) # number of successes

test.result2 <- binom.test(x = successes2,            # data
                           n = n2,                    # number of trials
                           p = 0.25,                 # p0 = 0.50 for each dogs indiv. trial ^ 2 trials = 0.25
                           alternative = "greater")  # one-sided
test.result2$p.value


[1] 9.536743e-07


The probability of all 10 dogs successfully retrieving the new toy in both trials is around 0.00000095.


2.3 Part c


Code
n <- 10   # number of trials
p <- 0.25 # prob of success

mu_Y    = n*p             # mean of gaussian approx.
sigma_Y = sqrt(n*p*(1-p)) # standard dev of gaussian approx.

# P(B=b) = P(b - 0.50 < Y < b + 0.50) = P(Y<= b + 0.50) - P(Y<= b - 0.50)
# P(B=10) = P(10 - 0.50 < Y < 10 + 0.50) = P(Y<= 10 + 0.50) - P(Y<= 10 - 0.50)
(prob <- pnorm(10.5, mu_Y, sigma_Y) - pnorm(9.5, mu_Y, sigma_Y))


[1] 1.567447e-07


Yes, the probability obtained from the gaussian distribution approximation is around the same as the probability obtained from the binomial distribution. 0.00000095  0.00000016.


2.4 Part d
I think that, because all of the trials were a success, performing an inference might not be the best option due to having zero variability in the sample. Doing this inference, with no variability, will reject the null hypothesis unless p0 lies above some threshold. This meeans that the inference has less to do with the data and more to do with the chosen null hypothesis.

title: Homework 2 – k Sample Inference
text:
1.1 Part a
Complete the following steps in \(R=1000\) simulations.

Simulate data for \(k=5\) samples \(n=30\) drawn from a standard Gaussian distribution.
Use pairwise.t.test(..., p.adjust.method="none") to compute unadjusted pairwise \(t\)-tests and record if any comparison yields statistically discernible support for a non-zero mean.
Use rstatix::tukey_hsd(...) to compute the Tukey’s HSD adjusted pairwise tests and record if any comparison yields statistically discernible support for a non-zero mean.

In the end, describe the Type I error rates.



Code
set.seed(1212)

k <- 5    # number of samples
n <- 30   # sample size
R <- 1000 # simulations

group <- factor(rep(1:k, each = n))

sig_none <- logical(R)
sig_tukey <- logical(R)

for (i in 1:R) {

  value <- rnorm(k * n, mean = 0, sd = 1)
  sim_data <- tibble(group = group, value = value)

  sig_none[i] <- any(pairwise.t.test(x = sim_data$value,
                                      g = sim_data$group,
                                      p.adjust.method = "none")$p.value < 0.05,
                      na.rm = TRUE)

  sig_tukey[i] <- any(tukey_hsd(aov(value ~ group, data = sim_data))$p.adj < 0.05)

}

# Type 1 error rates
mean(sig_none)


[1] 0.279


Code
mean(sig_tukey)


[1] 0.049



The Type 1 error rate for the uncorrected test is 27.9%, while the Type 1 error rate for the corrected test is 4.9%, which is close to 5%. This makes sense because the corrected test caps the FWER at \(\alpha = 0.05\). The uncorrected test has a much higher chance of detecting a difference when there is none (detecting noise) than the corrected test.

title: Homework 2 – k Sample Inference
text:
1.2 Part b
Redo the simulation, changing to adjust according to the false discovery rate p.adjust.method="BH" and comment on the differences.



Code
set.seed(1212)

k <- 5    # number of samples
n <- 30   # sample size
R <- 1000 # simulations

group <- factor(rep(1:k, each = n))

sig_bh <- logical(R)
sig_tukey <- logical(R)

for (i in 1:R) {

  value <- rnorm(k * n, mean = 0, sd = 1)
  sim_data <- tibble(group = group, value = value)

  sig_bh[i] <- any(pairwise.t.test(x = sim_data$value,
                                      g = sim_data$group,
                                      p.adjust.method = "BH")$p.value < 0.05,
                      na.rm = TRUE)

  sig_tukey[i] <- any(tukey_hsd(aov(value ~ group, data = sim_data))$p.adj < 0.05)

}

# Type 1 error rates
mean(sig_bh)


[1] 0.039


Code
mean(sig_tukey)


[1] 0.049


 The BH correction brought the Type 1 Error rate down a substantial amount to 0.039, towards \(\alpha = 0.05\) like the Tukey test. I notice that the BH correction is slightly lower than the Type 1 error rate for the Tukey test which was 0.049, but they are much closer than the simulation in Question 1.1. The reason that they might not be the same is because BH limits the proportion of false positives to 5% while the Tukey test limits FWER and the probability of making 1 Type 1 error at all to 5%, so they correct for different things.

title: Homework 2 – k Sample Inference
text:
2.1 Part a
Assume the researchers were targeting a moderate effect size of Cohen’s \(f = 0.25\), setting significance level \(\alpha = 0.05\) and desired power \(1 - \beta = 0.80\). Were they adequately powered?
Note: The actual effect size is \(f=0.55\), but researchers usually do not know that ahead of time and defaulted to moderate, instead of specifying a large effect.
What is the required sample size per group (\(n\)) and the overall total sample size (\(N\))? Write the R code using the pwr package to calculate this sample size. This package assumes all samples are of the same size so \(N=nk\), where \(k\) is the number of samples. Note that the best answers will have a corresponding graphical display.



Code
k <- 5         # Number of groups
f.mod <- 0.25  # moderate effect size using Cohen's f
alpha <- 0.05  # significance level

(n.small <- ceiling(pwr.anova.test(k = k,
                                   f = f.mod,
                                   sig.level = alpha,
                                   power = 0.80)$n))   # sample size per group


[1] 40


Code
N.small <- n.small * k   # total sample size

# Power curve across a range of n
power_curve <- tibble(n = seq(5, 60, by = 1)) |>
  mutate(power = map_dbl(n, ~ pwr.anova.test(k = k, n = .x, f = f.mod,
                                             sig.level = alpha)$power))

ggplot(power_curve, aes(x = n, y = power)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.80, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = n.small, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  labs(
    x = "Sample Size",
    y = "Power",
    title = "Power"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.line = element_line(color = "black"),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16)
  )









 The researchers need a sample size of at least n = 40 per group to achieve 80% power, so the MFAP4 study is adequately powered because the lowest group sample size was 67 (> 40). The total sample size needed is N = 200.

title: Homework 2 – k Sample Inference
text:
2.2 Part b
The project was funded by several agencies. Suppose that a funding agency suggested funding limiting the researchers to \(N=150\). Evaluate this suggestion in the context of the ANOVA. Would that be large enough to be adequately powered?
Compute the non-centrality parameter \[\lambda = k \cdot n \cdot f^2\] and use the non-central \(F\) distribution to compute the power under \(H_a\) for Cohen’s \(f = 0.25\). Calculate the statistical power achieved under this budget constraint. Note that the best answers will have a corresponding graphical display.



Code
k <- 5         # Number of groups
n <- 30        # sample size per group
f <- 0.25      # Cohen's f effect size
alpha <- 0.05  # significance level

(pwr.anova.test(k = k,
                n = n,
                f = 0.25,
                sig.level = alpha)$power)


[1] 0.6675964


Code
# non-centrality parameter for plotting
lambda <- k * n * f^2

df1 <- k - 1
df2 <- k * (n - 1)
F_crit <- qf(1 - alpha, df1, df2) # F-statistic

# x-axis range wide enough to show both curves fully
x_max <- qf(0.999, df1, df2, ncp = lambda) * 1.1
x <- seq(0, x_max, length.out = 1000)

dat <- tibble(
  x = x,
  null = df(x, df1, df2),
  alt  = df(x, df1, df2, ncp = lambda)
)

# Shaded regions
type_ii <- dat |>
  filter(x <= F_crit) |> 
  transmute(x, y = alt, region = "Type II Error")
power   <- dat |> 
  filter(x >= F_crit) |> 
  transmute(x, y = alt, region = "Power")
type_i  <- dat |> 
  filter(x >= F_crit) |> 
  transmute(x, y = null, region = "Type I Error")

regions <- bind_rows(type_ii, power, type_i) |>
  mutate(region = factor(region, levels = c("Power", "Type I Error", "Type II Error")))

ggplot() +
  geom_area(data = regions, aes(x = x, y = y, fill = region),
            alpha = 0.6, position = "identity") +
  geom_line(data = dat, aes(x = x, y = alt, color = "An Alternative Distribution"),
            linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_line(data = dat, aes(x = x, y = null, color = "Null Distribution"),
            linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Power" = "#E8C468",
                                "Type I Error" = "#B5524A",
                                "Type II Error" = "grey80")) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("An Alternative Distribution" = "black",
                                 "Null Distribution" = "darkred")) +
  labs(
    title = paste0("Moderate (f = ", f, ", k = ", k,
                    "); n per group = ", n, " (N = ", n * k, ")"),
    x = "F",
    y = "Density",
    fill = NULL,
    color = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    panel.border = element_rect(color = "black", fill = NA, linewidth = 0.7),
    legend.position = "right"
  )









 The statistical power with N = 150 from the budget constraint is around 67%, which does not meet the general rule of 80%.

title: Homework 2 – k Sample Inference
text:
2.3 Part c
In the article the researchers state:

However, the statistical power was not sufficient to allow an accurate discrimination of no to moderate stages of hepatic fibrosis (F0–F2) from severe fibrosis and cirrhosis (F3 and F4).

The European Association for the Study of the Liver (EASL) provides treatment recommendations based on these stages.

Stages 0-1: Treatment is deferred with regularly assessment
Stage 2: Treatment is justified for those in stage 2
Stage 3-4: Treatment is a priority for those in stages

Suppose the researcher wanted to perform a follow-up test where they want to ensure adequate power not just for the overall ANOVA \(F\)-test, but specifically to detect a pairwise differences between stages 1 and 2. Explain why the sample size computed in Part a may not be enough and use PMCMRplus::power.tukey.test() to compute a sample size that attains adequate power.
Note: The researchers would have had to do this a priori. Because we aren’t medical experts, you can use sample estimates using the original data. \[\begin{align*}
  n & = \text{answer from part a}\\
  \mu_{\Delta} & = 0.25 \\
  \sigma^2_{\text{pooled}} & = \frac{(176-1)0.85^2 + (135-1)0.84^2}{176+135-2} = 0.7152\\
  \sigma_{\text{within}}= 0.77
\end{align*}\]



Code
# parameters 
mu_delta <- 0.25
sigma_within <- 0.77
within_var <- sigma_within^2
alpha <- 0.05
groups <- k   # 5 groups

# search a wide enough range of n
n_seq <- n.small:400
tukey_power <- sapply(n_seq, function(n) {
  power.tukey.test(n = n, groups = groups, delta = mu_delta,
                    within.var = within_var, sig.level = alpha)$power
})

power_curve_tukey <- tibble(n = n_seq, power = tukey_power)

n_required_tukey <- n_seq[which(tukey_power >= 0.80)[1]]

ggplot(power_curve_tukey, aes(x = n, y = power)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.80, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = n_required_tukey, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  labs(
    x = "Sample Size per Group (n)",
    y = "Power",
    title = "Power for Detecting a Pairwise Difference (Tukey HSD)",
    subtitle = paste0("k = ", groups, ", \u03B4 = ", mu_delta,
                       ", \u03C3 = ", sigma_within,
                       "; required n = ", n_required_tukey)
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    panel.border = element_rect(color = "black", fill = NA, linewidth = 0.7),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14)
  )









 The required sample size for each group to achieve 80% on the pairwise comparison is n = 243. A sample size for each group of n = 40 achieves 80% for the overall ANOVA F-test, but not for a pairwise comparison due to the controlling of the FWER to 0.05 across all 10 comparisons. This increases the critical value and decreases alpha for each comparison, which in turn decreases power.

title: Homework 2 – k Sample Inference
text:
2.4 Part d
How does the answer to Part c change if they wanted to have adequate power for all pairwise comparisons? Use Superpower::ANOVA_design() to set up the ANOVA set up.
Note: Use design “5b” and the following. \[\begin{align*}
  \boldsymbol{\mu} &= \{2.92, 3.11, 3.36, 4.04, 4.35\}\\
  \sigma^2 &= \frac{(97-1)0.87^2 + (176-1)0.85^2 + (135-1)0.84^2 + (67-1)1.00^2 + (67-1)0.90^2}{97+176+135+67+67-5} = 0.80
\end{align*}\]
Compute the power of the researcher’s design (part a) using Superpower::ANOVA_power(). If the researchers were able to oversample by double, a common approach to addressing this issue, would their power be at least 80% for all pariwise comparisons?
Note: This code can take a minute. You may want to set cache: true in your R chunk yaml header. You will also see more power because the actual effect size was 0.55.



Code
# parameters 
mu = c(2.92, 3.11, 3.36, 4.04, 4.35)
var = 0.80

# design setup using ANOVA_design()
design_result <- ANOVA_design(design = "5b",
                              n = 40,
                              mu = mu,
                              sd = sqrt(var))









Code
# power test
ANOVA_power(design_result = design_result,
            alpha_level = 0.05,
            nsims = 1000, # simulate 1000 times
            p_adjust = "bonferroni",
            seed = 1234)

title: Homework 2 – k Sample Inference
text:
3.5 Part e
Write a short paragraph directly addressing the researcher’s hypothesis using your work in (a)-(d).
After conducting a Welch’s ANOVA test, we found statistically discernible support that at least one group (2M, 6M, 16M, and 16M_Tx) had a different mean SUVmax from the others (\(p = 0.00069\)). After conducting a post-hoc analysis using a Games Howell test for multiple comparisons, we found that, among the 3 control groups, the mean SUVmax in male mice increases from 2 months to 6 months to 16 months (\(p = 0.012\) and \(p = 0.008\), respectively). Additionally, we found that the 16 month treatment group experienced a discernibly lower SUVmax than the 16 month control group (\(p = 0.043\)) and that it was comparable to the SUVmax of the 2 month group (\(p = 0.308\)) and the 6 month group (\(p = 0.698\)). Overall, our data support that SUVmax increases with age, and that a low-dose nicotine treatment can lower SUVmax in older mice to levels similar to that of younger mice. A major limitation to consider from this study is that we only observed 3 samples per group; further research should be aimed at acquiring more samples to increase the statistical power of the study.

title: Homework 2 – k Sample Inference
text:
1.1 Part a
Complete the following steps in \(R=1000\) simulations.

Simulate data for \(k=5\) samples \(n=30\) drawn from a standard Gaussian distribution.
Use pairwise.t.test(..., p.adjust.method="none") to compute unadjusted pairwise \(t\)-tests and record if any comparison yields statistically discernible support for a non-zero mean.
Use rstatix::tukey_hsd(...) to compute the Tukey’s HSD adjusted pairwise tests and record if any comparison yields statistically discernible support for a non-zero mean.

In the end, describe the Type I error rates.



Code
set.seed(1212)

k <- 5    # number of samples
n <- 30   # sample size
R <- 1000 # simulations

group <- factor(rep(1:k, each = n))

sig_none <- logical(R)
sig_tukey <- logical(R)

for (i in 1:R) {

  value <- rnorm(k * n, mean = 0, sd = 1)
  sim_data <- tibble(group = group, value = value)

  sig_none[i] <- any(pairwise.t.test(x = sim_data$value,
                                      g = sim_data$group,
                                      p.adjust.method = "none")$p.value < 0.05,
                      na.rm = TRUE)

  sig_tukey[i] <- any(tukey_hsd(aov(value ~ group, data = sim_data))$p.adj < 0.05)

}

# Type 1 error rates
mean(sig_none)


[1] 0.279


Code
mean(sig_tukey)


[1] 0.049



The Type 1 error rate for the uncorrected test is 27.9%, while the Type 1 error rate for the corrected test is 4.9%, which is close to 5%. This makes sense because the corrected test caps the FWER at \(\alpha = 0.05\). The uncorrected test has a much higher chance of detecting a difference when there is none (detecting noise) than the corrected test.

n <- 30   # sample size
R <- 1000 # simulations

group <- factor(rep(1:k, each = n))

sig_bh <- logical(R)
sig_tukey <- logical(R)

for (i in 1:R) {

                      na.rm = TRUE)

}

# Type 1 error rates
mean(sig_bh)


[1] 0.039


Code
mean(sig_tukey)


[1] 0.049


 The BH correction brought the Type 1 Error rate down a substantial amount to 0.039, towards \(\alpha = 0.05\) like the Tukey test. I notice that the BH correction is slightly lower than the Type 1 error rate for the Tukey test which was 0.049, but they are much closer than the simulation in Question 1.1. The reason that they might not be the same is because BH limits the proportion of false positives to 5% while the Tukey test limits FWER and the probability of making 1 Type 1 error at all to 5%, so they correct for different things.

2.1 Part a
Assume the researchers were targeting a moderate effect size of Cohen’s \(f = 0.25\), setting significance level \(\alpha = 0.05\) and desired power \(1 - \beta = 0.80\). Were they adequately powered?
Note: The actual effect size is \(f=0.55\), but researchers usually do not know that ahead of time and defaulted to moderate, instead of specifying a large effect.
What is the required sample size per group (\(n\)) and the overall total sample size (\(N\))? Write the R code using the pwr package to calculate this sample size. This package assumes all samples are of the same size so \(N=nk\), where \(k\) is the number of samples. Note that the best answers will have a corresponding graphical display.



Code
k <- 5         # Number of groups
f.mod <- 0.25  # moderate effect size using Cohen's f
alpha <- 0.05  # significance level

(n.small <- ceiling(pwr.anova.test(k = k,
                                   f = f.mod,
                                   sig.level = alpha,
                                   power = 0.80)$n))   # sample size per group


[1] 40


Code
N.small <- n.small * k   # total sample size

# Power curve across a range of n
power_curve <- tibble(n = seq(5, 60, by = 1)) |>
  mutate(power = map_dbl(n, ~ pwr.anova.test(k = k, n = .x, f = f.mod,
                                             sig.level = alpha)$power))

ggplot(power_curve, aes(x = n, y = power)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.80, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = n.small, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +

    x = "Sample Size",
    y = "Power",
    title = "Power"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.line = element_line(color = "black"),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16)
  )

2.2 Part b
The project was funded by several agencies. Suppose that a funding agency suggested funding limiting the researchers to \(N=150\). Evaluate this suggestion in the context of the ANOVA. Would that be large enough to be adequately powered?
Compute the non-centrality parameter \[\lambda = k \cdot n \cdot f^2\] and use the non-central \(F\) distribution to compute the power under \(H_a\) for Cohen’s \(f = 0.25\). Calculate the statistical power achieved under this budget constraint. Note that the best answers will have a corresponding graphical display.



Code
k <- 5         # Number of groups
n <- 30        # sample size per group
f <- 0.25      # Cohen's f effect size
alpha <- 0.05  # significance level

(pwr.anova.test(k = k,
                n = n,
                f = 0.25,
                sig.level = alpha)$power)


[1] 0.6675964


Code
# non-centrality parameter for plotting
lambda <- k * n * f^2

df1 <- k - 1
df2 <- k * (n - 1)
F_crit <- qf(1 - alpha, df1, df2) # F-statistic

# x-axis range wide enough to show both curves fully
x_max <- qf(0.999, df1, df2, ncp = lambda) * 1.1
x <- seq(0, x_max, length.out = 1000)

dat <- tibble(
  x = x,
  null = df(x, df1, df2),
  alt  = df(x, df1, df2, ncp = lambda)
)

# Shaded regions
type_ii <- dat |>
  filter(x <= F_crit) |> 
  transmute(x, y = alt, region = "Type II Error")
power   <- dat |> 
  filter(x >= F_crit) |> 
  transmute(x, y = alt, region = "Power")
type_i  <- dat |> 
  filter(x >= F_crit) |> 
  transmute(x, y = null, region = "Type I Error")

regions <- bind_rows(type_ii, power, type_i) |>
  mutate(region = factor(region, levels = c("Power", "Type I Error", "Type II Error")))

ggplot() +
  geom_area(data = regions, aes(x = x, y = y, fill = region),
            alpha = 0.6, position = "identity") +
  geom_line(data = dat, aes(x = x, y = alt, color = "An Alternative Distribution"),
            linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_line(data = dat, aes(x = x, y = null, color = "Null Distribution"),
            linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Power" = "#E8C468",
                                "Type I Error" = "#B5524A",
                                "Type II Error" = "grey80")) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("An Alternative Distribution" = "black",
                                 "Null Distribution" = "darkred")) +
  labs(
    title = paste0("Moderate (f = ", f, ", k = ", k,
                    "); n per group = ", n, " (N = ", n * k, ")"),
    x = "F",
    y = "Density",
    fill = NULL,
    color = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    panel.border = element_rect(color = "black", fill = NA, linewidth = 0.7),
    legend.position = "right"
  )









 The statistical power with N = 150 from the budget constraint is around 67%, which does not meet the general rule of 80%.

text:
2.3 Part c
In the article the researchers state:

However, the statistical power was not sufficient to allow an accurate discrimination of no to moderate stages of hepatic fibrosis (F0–F2) from severe fibrosis and cirrhosis (F3 and F4).

The European Association for the Study of the Liver (EASL) provides treatment recommendations based on these stages.

Stages 0-1: Treatment is deferred with regularly assessment
Stage 2: Treatment is justified for those in stage 2
Stage 3-4: Treatment is a priority for those in stages

Suppose the researcher wanted to perform a follow-up test where they want to ensure adequate power not just for the overall ANOVA \(F\)-test, but specifically to detect a pairwise differences between stages 1 and 2. Explain why the sample size computed in Part a may not be enough and use PMCMRplus::power.tukey.test() to compute a sample size that attains adequate power.
Note: The researchers would have had to do this a priori. Because we aren’t medical experts, you can use sample estimates using the original data. \[\begin{align*}
  n & = \text{answer from part a}\\
  \mu_{\Delta} & = 0.25 \\
  \sigma^2_{\text{pooled}} & = \frac{(176-1)0.85^2 + (135-1)0.84^2}{176+135-2} = 0.7152\\
  \sigma_{\text{within}}= 0.77
\end{align*}\]



Code
# parameters 
mu_delta <- 0.25
sigma_within <- 0.77
within_var <- sigma_within^2
alpha <- 0.05
groups <- k   # 5 groups

# search a wide enough range of n
n_seq <- n.small:400
tukey_power <- sapply(n_seq, function(n) {
  power.tukey.test(n = n, groups = groups, delta = mu_delta,
                    within.var = within_var, sig.level = alpha)$power
})

power_curve_tukey <- tibble(n = n_seq, power = tukey_power)

n_required_tukey <- n_seq[which(tukey_power >= 0.80)[1]]

ggplot(power_curve_tukey, aes(x = n, y = power)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.80, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = n_required_tukey, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  labs(
    x = "Sample Size per Group (n)",
    y = "Power",
    title = "Power for Detecting a Pairwise Difference (Tukey HSD)",
    subtitle = paste0("k = ", groups, ", \u03B4 = ", mu_delta,
                       ", \u03C3 = ", sigma_within,
                       "; required n = ", n_required_tukey)
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    panel.border = element_rect(color = "black", fill = NA, linewidth = 0.7),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14)
  )









 The required sample size for each group to achieve 80% on the pairwise comparison is n = 243. A sample size for each group of n = 40 achieves 80% for the overall ANOVA F-test, but not for a pairwise comparison due to the controlling of the FWER to 0.05 across all 10 comparisons. This increases the critical value and decreases alpha for each comparison, which in turn decreases power.

text:
3.5 Part e
Write a short paragraph directly addressing the researcher’s hypothesis using your work in (a)-(d).
After conducting a Welch’s ANOVA test, we found statistically discernible support that at least one group (2M, 6M, 16M, and 16M_Tx) had a different mean SUVmax from the others (\(p = 0.00069\)). After conducting a post-hoc analysis using a Games Howell test for multiple comparisons, we found that, among the 3 control groups, the mean SUVmax in male mice increases from 2 months to 6 months to 16 months (\(p = 0.012\) and \(p = 0.008\), respectively). Additionally, we found that the 16 month treatment group experienced a discernibly lower SUVmax than the 16 month control group (\(p = 0.043\)) and that it was comparable to the SUVmax of the 2 month group (\(p = 0.308\)) and the 6 month group (\(p = 0.698\)). Overall, our data support that SUVmax increases with age, and that a low-dose nicotine treatment can lower SUVmax in older mice to levels similar to that of younger mice. A major limitation to consider from this study is that we only observed 3 samples per group; further research should be aimed at acquiring more samples to increase the statistical power of the study.
